Subject: Concurrency failure modes and scaling — initial questions

Hi Neha,

Thanks for taking our RFI. A few items we need clarity on to validate performance claims for procurement:

1) Under sustained high concurrency (500–2,000 concurrent chat sessions) what are the common failure modes you observe (queue drops, OOMs, request timeouts, degraded generations)?
2) How does Redwood quantify graceful degradation when autoscaling cannot keep up (e.g., model fallbacks, reduced max_tokens, early termination)?
3) For a 99.95% availability SLA target, what test harness and traffic patterns would you recommend to demonstrate compliance?

We've attached our baseline traffic samples and a sample payload (attachment: globex-sample-load.json). Please include any assumptions (max seq length, typical prompt size) in your response.

Appreciate a concise response we can include in the RFI packet.

Best,
Samir

Subject: Re: Concurrency failure modes and scaling — initial questions

Hi Samir — thanks for the clear questions and the sample payload. High level answers first, then a short recommended test plan.

High-level failure modes we observe (short list):
- Queueing backpressure: when request arrival exceeds configured concurrency/batching window; mitigated by adaptive batching and shedding lower-priority requests.
- Memory pressure / OOM on long-sequence hot paths: typically triggered by unexpectedly large seq_len or chat context retention; mitigated by prefix cache eviction and sequence truncation policies.
- Token generation timeouts (client-level): caused when generation exceeds per-request token-time budget due to long generations or extreme sampling; mitigated by early-stop heuristics and response streaming.
- Transient node restart due to GPU failure: handled by autoscaling + request rerouting to spare nodes.

Graceful degradation behaviors we provide:
- Model tier fallback: automatic routing to a quantized or smaller variant when larger model pool is saturated.
- Token budget enforcement: per-request max_tokens and dynamic truncation when queueing detected.
- Priority queues: separation of latency-SLO routes vs. best-effort workloads.

Recommended test harness (short):
1) Traffic mix: ramp to steady-state concurrency target, then inject 30–60s bursts at 2–3x to exercise autoscaler. Use mixture: 70% short prompts (~40 tokens), 30% long prompts (~800 tokens).
2) Stability window: run soak for 2 hours at steady-state target to confirm tail-latency distributions and cache behavior.
3) Failure injection: kill 1–2 serving nodes mid-soak to validate routing and fallback.
4) Observability: collect per-token latency histograms, queue depths, GPU mem utilization, and model-switch events.

Assumptions: typical prompt size 40–800 tokens, average 120 tokens output. Sequence length cap used in our tests: 1,024 tokens.

I'll loop in Rishi with details of the KV-cache and batch sizing we recommend. Attached a short playbook (redwood-concurrency-playbook.pdf) and our test config templates.

Best,
Neha Kapoor
Enterprise Solutions — Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Concurrency failure modes and scaling — KV cache and batching details

Samir / Neha — quick technical notes you can include in the RFI appendix.

1) KV cache behavior: under high-concurrency chat workloads we keep per-session KV caches pinned to the serving shard; cache hit rates >85% for conversational flows reduce per-token compute by ~40% in our internal tests. Eviction is LRU with TTL tunables per-tenant.

2) Batching strategy: we use a continuous-batching window (configurable 8–40 ms) that trades latency for throughput. For SLO-focused routes we bias towards 8–12 ms; for cost-focused routes we use 20–40 ms and higher max batch sizes.

3) Tail-latency mitigation: a few recommended levers — dynamic per-request priority, quick-fail for requests exceeding token/time budget, and shadowing to pre-warm caches for heavy conversational cohorts.

4) Expected degradation envelope: when autoscaler lags during a 2x sudden sustained spike you should expect 95th->99.9th percentile latency to increase by ~2–5x depending on prompt length and batching window; model fallback typically contains 99.9th percentile growth to <3x baseline in our controlled tests.

If you want numbers for your specific sample payload I can run a targeted synthetic workload; we'll need CSV of per-session lengths and a short run window (30–60 minutes).

Thanks,
Rishi
Head of Performance — Redwood Inference

Thanks Neha & Rishi — very helpful. A couple of follow-ups before we escalate to procurement: 

- Can you outline the exact test methodology and success criteria you'd use to certify a Dedicated pool for our traffic shape? We'll include this in our procurement test plan.
- Does Redwood support an automated failover to a smaller/quantized model without semantic regression checks? We want to understand risk of correctness loss during fallback.
- Proposal: a 2-week PoC with a 1TB dataset of anonymized chat transcripts (we will transfer) and a 3-hour daily soak at peak concurrency for the second week. Please confirm minimal Redwood engineering time required and any prerequisites (VPC peering, access controls).

Can Marissa or Dev advise on contract-level constraints (SOW, entitlements) — copying contracting.

Best,
Samir

Subject: Re: Concurrency failure modes and scaling — PoC scope and schedule

Samir — proposed quick plan and assumptions below.

PoC summary (2 weeks):
- Week 1: Integration and baseline runs. Redwood will validate dataset ingestion, establish VPC peering (if private), and run short load sweeps to tune batching and cache TTLs.
- Week 2: Soak at agreed peak concurrency (3 hours daily) + a 2-hour sustained 2x spike test to exercise autoscaler and failover.

Success criteria (example):
- 99.9% of requests during soak complete under your target latency (you to define; suggest 500 ms for short prompts, 2s for long prompts).
- No OOM events; any node restarts must complete within configured capacity failover window without >1% request loss.
- Automatic model fallback triggered without >10% semantic drift on a small human-eval prompt set (we will run a 100-sample regression).

Engineering footprint: we estimate 3 engineer-days of Redwood engagement for Week 1 (onboarding + tuning) and 2 engineer-days during Week 2 (run support & postmortem). Additional SOW items (VPC peering, KMS access, schedule) to be included in an addendum.

Attachments: concurrency-sim-specs.yaml (test script), a checklist of prerequisites is at the Drive link shared previously.

If that aligns, Neha / Marissa will prepare SOW language & timelines for contracting.

Regards,
Dev Patel
Solution Architect — Redwood Inference
